edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Sed de ipso Apostolo revolvunt, quod dixerit: Non enim me ad tinguendum Christus misit, quasi hoc argumento Baptismus adimatur. Cur enim tinxit Gaium et Crispum et Stephanae domum? Quanquam etsi non eum miserat Christus ad tinguendum, tamen aliis Apostolis praeceperat tinguere. Verum haec pro conditione tunc temporis ad Corinthios scripta sunt, quoniam schismata et dissensiones inter illos movebantur, dum alius Paulo deputat, alius Apollo. Propter quod pacificus Apostolus, ne sibi omnia defendere videretur, non ad tinguendum ait se missum, sed ad praedicandum. Nam et prius est praedicare, posterius tinguere. Si prius praedicatum: puto autem licuit et tinguere cui licuit praedicare.
pass_a_gloss: But they bring up against the Apostle himself what he said: For Christ did not send me to baptize, as if by this argument Baptism is taken away. Why did he baptize Gaius and Crispus and the household of Stephanas? Although even if Christ had not sent him to baptize, nevertheless he had instructed the other Apostles to baptize. But these things were written to the Corinthians at that time on account of the condition, since schisms and dissensions were being stirred up among them, while one was devoted to Paul, another to Apollo. On account of which the peaceful Apostle, lest he seem to be defending everything for himself, says he was not sent to baptize, but to preach. For to preach is prior, to baptize is posterior. If something has been preached beforehand: I think, however, it was also permitted to baptize whoever was permitted to preach.

pass_b_english: They drag the Apostle's own words into court: "Christ did not send me to baptize" (1 Cor 1:17), as if that single line cancels baptism altogether. If the argument holds, why did he baptize Gaius, Crispus, and the whole household of Stephanas (1 Cor 1:14-16)? Even granting that Christ did not commission him personally to baptize, he had ordered the other Apostles to do exactly that. Paul wrote these words to Corinth under pressure; schisms and party spirit were tearing the church apart, some claiming Paul, others Apollos. To keep the peace and avoid looking like he was feathering his own nest, the Apostle says he was sent to preach, not to baptize. Preaching comes first, baptism follows; and I would argue that whoever is authorized to preach is also authorized to baptize.

review.notes: The translation accurately reflects the Latin text. Pass B correctly identifies and adds the necessary scripture citations (1 Cor 1:17 and 1 Cor 1:14-16) for the quoted/alluded clauses, which is required. The translation of 'ne sibi omnia defendere videretur' as 'to avoid looking like he was feathering his own nest' is a valid idiomatic rendering of the sense in Pass B, and Pass A's 'lest he seem to be defending everything for himself' is also faithful.
